title: Ruff in a Nutshell + Configuring it on VsCode
text:
Hello guys!
Today I want to talk about RUFF, my default formatter (and much more) for Python language.
In a nutshell, RUFF can be seen as a tool that performs all these tasks:
RUFF = Flake8 + isort + black + pydocstyle + pyupgrade + autoflake
Flake8 = Linter, which reports style + syntax errors
isort = Sort the imports
black = formatter ; mostly PEP8 compliant, but with a default line-length of 88 instead of PEP 8’s 79. It handles single/double quotes, empty lines and parentheses
pydocstyle = docstrings
pyupgrade = upgrade syntax for newer python versions
autoflake = Remove unused imports and unused variables
So, instead of having to set up each one individually, use RUFF and have all these tools into a single one. RUFF was written in rust, so it is not a wrap of the previously mentioned. Also, it is way faster than the previous tools.

title: Ruff in a Nutshell + Configuring it on VsCode
Ruff in a Nutshell + Configuring it on VsCode
text:
Bonus (Caveat)
I struggled to start using a tool like this because I used to write code in a single long line. I always received the E501: line-too-long warning from pycodestyle/Flake8. It happens when a line is longer than 79 characters, which is the recommendation in PEP 8 (ruff, like black, uses a slightly larger default of 88 characters). After applying a tool like ruff my code changed drastically (as it would force me to break lines), and it was uncomfortable in the beginning. So, I started to relax the parameter of the line-length a little bit (from the default to, for example, 150 characters) and started to analyze the impact of change. Then I realized that the impact on my previous code was not large at all.
Leaving the limit as the default, PEP 8 argues that you can open multiple files side by side, making also easier to see the git diff changes.
Anyway, if you think that this limit is small, you can relax it a little bit globally, doing it by:
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 130 # E501 (line-too-long) now only warns above 130 characters

lint.ignore = [
    "E701", # Ignore single-line if statements
]
lint.extend-select = ["D"] # Enable the docstring rules (pydocstyle), which are off by default
extend-include = ["*.ipynb"]

[tool.ruff.format]
quote-style = "double"
docstring-code-format = true

[tool.ruff.lint.pydocstyle] # Docstring style that the "D" rules check against
convention = "google"
Or, if you only want to keep a few specific lines as they are:

Add # noqa: E501 at the end of a line, so the linter stops warning that it is too long.
Add # fmt: skip at the end of a line, so the formatter does not reformat it.
Wrap a block of code between # fmt: off and # fmt: on, so the formatter leaves the whole block untouched.

Happy coding.

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
text: Hello guys! I want to talk a widely used metric, specially in time series modelling, which it is MAPE.

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
text:
Why MAPE is used
MAPE is a largely used metric because has the following benefits:

It is a percentage metric; so, it can be used to compare time series with different units.
It is largely used. People specially from other fields use it without knowing that are using it because it is so straight forward and natural.

I will give an example for the last bit: Let’s suppose that a salesperson had to sell 100 pairs of boots, but he sold 80, so how far is he from the target? Well, (80-100)/100 = -0,20 = -20%. So the salesperson is 20% far from the target. The formula for MAPE can be described as:
\[\text{MAPE} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left| \frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{y_i} \right|}{n}\]
where:

\(y_i\) is the true value of observation \(i\) (y_true);
\(\hat{y}_i\) is the predicted value of observation \(i\) (y_pred);
\(n\) is the number of observations.

It is so intuitive. However, behind this popularity, MAPE has several pitfalls, specially when working with high number of time series at the same time:

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
text:
MAPE is a biased metric:
To give a simple example, let’s suppose that our y_pred is 100; if the y_true is 150, we have a MAPE equals to 0.33, in contrast to MAPE equals 1 if y_true is 50. So, MAPE will always push toward to biased underforecasting.
See Table 1, which illustrates this:

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
section: MAPE is not defined when y_true is zero
text:
MAPE is not defined when y_true is zero
The denominator of mape is y_true. So, MAPE might return NaN on your programming software or Inf. In order to “fix” it, what many people do is to set y_true to a small value near to zero, which is what sklearn.metrics.mean_absolute_percentage_error do (setting y_true to \(2.22*10^-16\) when y_true is zero). But it gives other problems:

Setting y_true to \(2.22*10^-16\) will lead to a even higher MAPE number;
You will never know a “true” value of the error for this series;
Your prediction will be compromised even if your predictions are really good (let’s say 0.00001);
If you need to aggregate the metric of this series with other series, your comparison will be compromised because the resulting MAPE will be towards a very high number.

In practical terms, see in Table 2 how MAPE will behave if for a y_true of 0, we set 2.22E-16 for the last two rows of the table:

Others also don’t calculate the forecast for these points, but you will end up with same problem as number 2.

title: MAPE and its pitfalls
section: MAPE does not minimizes the error towards the mean value
text:
MAPE does not minimizes the error towards the mean value
This is not a pitfall, but it is a warning, because usually people want to be right on average, and this is not what MAPE does. In contrast, it will give a prediction towards a biased median, if I can so.
A very good resource to read about is shortcomings of MAPE, that will lead to many other resources.

title: Is Python an Interpreted language?
text: This is part 2 of a series. Read Part 1 first.

title: Is Python an Interpreted language?
text:
1 Quick questions
Right now, I will dive into specific questions that come up when writing Python code:

1.1 Why is Numpy faster than pure Python code?
It happens because Numpy is vectorized, while Python does not. And by vectorized, it means that the code will pass through the interpreter only once and all the routine will be executed in a loop in C; instead of invoking the interpreter on every iteration of a regular Python for loop.
Moreover, NumPy arrays use unboxed, contiguous, C-native buffers — more on why that matters in Section 1.2.
I will show an example in order to make it clearer:

import dis
import numpy as np
import time


def pure_python_version(n):
   total = 0.0
   for i in range(n):
      total += i * i
   return total


def numpy_version(n):
   arr = np.arange(n, dtype=np.float64)
   return np.sum(arr * arr)


N = 100_000_000

start = time.perf_counter()
result_py = pure_python_version(N)
py_time = time.perf_counter() - start

print("=" * 60)
print(f"PURE PYTHON VERSION THAT TOOK {round(py_time, 2)} seconds in BYTECODE")
print("=" * 60)
dis.dis(pure_python_version)

start = time.perf_counter()
result_numpy = numpy_version(N)
numpy_time = time.perf_counter() - start

print()
print("=" * 60)
print(f"NUMPY VERSION THAT TOOK {round(numpy_time, 2)} seconds in BYTECODE")
print("=" * 60)
dis.dis(numpy_version)

============================================================
PURE PYTHON VERSION THAT TOOK 16.59 seconds in BYTECODE
============================================================
  6           0 RESUME                   0

  7           2 LOAD_CONST               1 (0.0)
              4 STORE_FAST               1 (total)

  8           6 LOAD_GLOBAL              1 (NULL + range)
             16 LOAD_FAST                0 (n)
             18 CALL                     1
             26 GET_ITER
        >>   28 FOR_ITER                10 (to 52)
             32 STORE_FAST               2 (i)

  9          34 LOAD_FAST                1 (total)
             36 LOAD_FAST                2 (i)
             38 LOAD_FAST                2 (i)
             40 BINARY_OP                5 (*)
             44 BINARY_OP               13 (+=)
             48 STORE_FAST               1 (total)
             50 JUMP_BACKWARD           12 (to 28)

  8     >>   52 END_FOR

 10          54 LOAD_FAST                1 (total)
             56 RETURN_VALUE

============================================================
NUMPY VERSION THAT TOOK 2.6 seconds in BYTECODE
============================================================
 13           0 RESUME                   0

 14           2 LOAD_GLOBAL              0 (np)
             12 LOAD_ATTR                3 (NULL|self + arange)
             32 LOAD_FAST                0 (n)
             34 LOAD_GLOBAL              0 (np)
             44 LOAD_ATTR                4 (float64)
             64 KW_NAMES                 1 (('dtype',))
             66 CALL                     2
             74 STORE_FAST               1 (arr)

 15          76 LOAD_GLOBAL              0 (np)
             86 LOAD_ATTR                7 (NULL|self + sum)
            106 LOAD_FAST                1 (arr)
            108 LOAD_FAST                1 (arr)
            110 BINARY_OP                5 (*)
            114 CALL                     1
            122 RETURN_VALUE


I am not an expert on bytecode instructions in Python, but see that for pure Python, there is an operation called FOR_ITER that goes to L2, and then, it returns to L1, which is the loop itself.
When we look at the Numpy version, the for loop is gone, and all instructions run only once, not N times.


1.2 Why is C generally faster than Python?

C does not have an interpreter; it dispatches all code ahead of time into machine code during compilation;
Defining the variable types at declaration makes the code’s memory layout known to the machine ahead of time:

It does not have to make Runtime type checking.
It can calculate in advance how much of memory the operation will take, and optimize it.

Python values are boxed — every int/float is a full object with type info and a reference count, not a raw number sitting in memory. C works directly with raw bytes, no wrapper.

In order to exemplify the third point, I will run an example to show how many bytes a Python integer uses:

import sys

x = 5
print(f"type(x)        = {type(x)}")
print(f"sys.getsizeof(x)   = {sys.getsizeof(x)} bytes")

type(x)        = <class 'int'>
sys.getsizeof(x)   = 28 bytes


It uses 28 bytes, against 4 (or 8) in C (normally), which: + 8 bytes is used to save its reference count (it counts how many variables are referencing to it); + 8 bytes for the type pointer (so that the interpreter knows the basic operations available on this variable); + 8 bytes for the size field; + 4 bytes for the cost of each additional digital chunk


1.3 If I annotate my functions, will my code run faster?
NO. It happens because CPython ignores all type hints during compilation. See that in the below example the bytecode is the same:

import dis
import time


def add_no_hint(a, b):
    return a + b


def add_with_hint(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b


print("=== WITHOUT type hint ===")
dis.dis(add_no_hint)
print()
print("=== WITH type hint ===")
dis.dis(add_with_hint)

=== WITHOUT type hint ===
  5           0 RESUME                   0

  6           2 LOAD_FAST                0 (a)
              4 LOAD_FAST                1 (b)
              6 BINARY_OP                0 (+)
             10 RETURN_VALUE

=== WITH type hint ===
  9           0 RESUME                   0

 10           2 LOAD_FAST                0 (a)
              4 LOAD_FAST                1 (b)
              6 BINARY_OP                0 (+)
             10 RETURN_VALUE


Happy coding!

title: Is Python a Statically or Dynamically Typed Language?
text:
Today, I am going to talk about intrinsic characteristics of Python.
Have you ever received a TypeError while running your Python program?
It occurs because Python is a dynamic type language. It means the language verifies variable types during execution (runtime) - not during compilation, even though Python does compile your code into bytecode before running it. The type check only happens the instant an operation is actually executed, not when the code is first parsed and compiled.
Let’s go with an example:
def python_dynamic_language_example(execute_invalid_operation):
    print("The function was compiled to bytecode already")

    if execute_invalid_operation:
        a = 5
        b = "5"
        return a + b
    return "No invalid operation was found"
This function can run successfully even though there is an invalid operation inside the if clause:
python_dynamic_language_example(False)

The function was compiled to bytecode already


'No invalid operation was found'
Moreover, since this is a Quarto document, the mere fact that the whole .qmd file compiled successfully already shows the function was compiled to bytecode without error.
However, when we try to access the code portion that does the calculation, we receive the TypeError:
python_dynamic_language_example(True)

The function was compiled to bytecode already



---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[3], line 1
----> 1 python_dynamic_language_example(True)

Cell In[1], line 7, in python_dynamic_language_example(execute_invalid_operation)
      3 
      4     if execute_invalid_operation:
      5         a = 5
      6         b = "5"
----> 7         return a + b
      8     return "No invalid operation was found"

TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
which means that Python did not perform the operation because it was operated between two invalid types, even though it was compiled, as can be seen by dis:
import dis
dis.dis(python_dynamic_language_example)

  1           0 RESUME                   0

  2           2 LOAD_GLOBAL              1 (NULL + print)
             12 LOAD_CONST               1 ('The function was compiled to bytecode already')
             14 CALL                     1
             22 POP_TOP

  4          24 LOAD_FAST                0 (execute_invalid_operation)
             26 POP_JUMP_IF_FALSE        9 (to 46)

  5          28 LOAD_CONST               2 (5)
             30 STORE_FAST               1 (a)

  6          32 LOAD_CONST               3 ('5')
             34 STORE_FAST               2 (b)

  7          36 LOAD_FAST                1 (a)
             38 LOAD_FAST                2 (b)
             40 BINARY_OP                0 (+)
             44 RETURN_VALUE

  8     >>   46 RETURN_CONST             4 ('No invalid operation was found')
The fact that Python compiled this code, it means that it is dynamically type, instead of statically typed:
The fact that Python did not allow that operation occur in runtime means that it is strongly typed, instead of weakly typed:
Having these concepts in mind can help you to think on which language to use, or anticipate errors.

title: Is Python a Statically or Dynamically Typed Language?
text:
Flexibility in Python
Even though this is an odd behavior in Python, it allows you the change the variable type while programming:

a = 5
print(type(a))
print(id(a))
a = "5"
print(type(a))
print(id(a))

<class 'int'>
103300731305384
<class 'str'>
103300731366408


It occurs because the value has a type (dynamic type language), not the variable. It also allows you to write less boilerplate code, and make your code into production faster.

title: Is Python a Statically or Dynamically Typed Language?
section: What if you want to put more restrictions in Python ?
text:
What if you want to put more restrictions in Python ?
In recent Python versions (3.x), what you can do is add type annotation to variables and output of functions. However, it will still allow the function to be compiled:

def python_dynamic_language_example_typed(
    execute_invalid_operation: bool,
) -> str | TypeError:
    print("The function was compiled to bytecode already")

    if execute_invalid_operation:
        a: int = 5
        b: str = "5"
        return a + b
    return "No invalid"


dis.dis(python_dynamic_language_example_typed)

  1           0 RESUME                   0

  4           2 LOAD_GLOBAL              1 (NULL + print)
             12 LOAD_CONST               1 ('The function was compiled to bytecode already')
             14 CALL                     1
             22 POP_TOP

  6          24 LOAD_FAST                0 (execute_invalid_operation)
             26 POP_JUMP_IF_FALSE        9 (to 46)

  7          28 LOAD_CONST               2 (5)
             30 STORE_FAST               1 (a)

  8          32 LOAD_CONST               3 ('5')
             34 STORE_FAST               2 (b)

  9          36 LOAD_FAST                1 (a)
             38 LOAD_FAST                2 (b)
             40 BINARY_OP                0 (+)
             44 RETURN_VALUE

 10     >>   46 RETURN_CONST             4 ('No invalid')


However, if you are coding in an editor and uses a tool that does live checking, such as Pylance in Vs Code in standard mode, it would warn you about the operation:







and you could fix it right away.
These are concepts that you may not even realize that are important unless you know it.
Happy coding!

title: A história do Campeonato Brasileiro em números
text:
Critérios adotados no relatório
Categorias

As categorias que existiram em uma única edição foram reunidas com a mais próxima: o Sub-20 (2008) entra no Sub-18 e o Infantil (1994) entra no Sub-15. Em 2008 não houve Sub-18 e em 1994 ainda não havia Sub-15, então não há sobreposição.
O filtro “Sub-15 + Sub-18” soma as duas categorias de base.

Participantes

Conta-se cada linha da classificação final. Seis botonistas jogaram duas categorias na mesma edição e aparecem uma vez em cada uma: Faoro (SP, 1997), Rogério (PR, 1998), Robertinho (PR, 2000) e Pedro (PR, 2003), no Adulto e no Sub-18; Bruno (PR, 2005) e Vinícius (SP, 2006), no Adulto e no Sub-15. Nos rankings de participações, cada edição conta uma única vez por pessoa.
Em 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1996 e 1999 o histórico publica só parte da classificação. Esses anos são marcados como incompletos quando a classificação tem menos de 90% dos participantes informados pela organização ou menos de 60 nomes.
Não houve campeonato em 2020 e 2021, por causa da pandemia. Esses anos aparecem no eixo dos gráficos, sem dados.

Divisões e títulos

As divisões mudaram de nome (Ouro, Prata, Bronze, Extra e Copa → 1ª a 5ª Divisão). A comparação é feita pelo nível da divisão no ano: nível 1 é a principal (Série Ouro, 1ª Divisão ou divisão única).
Título = 1º lugar na divisão principal da categoria. Quando o filtro reúne mais de uma categoria, os títulos de todas elas têm o mesmo peso e são somados.

Gols e aproveitamento

Média de gols por partida = soma dos gols pró ÷ número de partidas (soma dos jogos de todos os botonistas ÷ 2).
Aproveitamento = pontos ÷ (3 × jogos).
Só entram os anos em que o histórico traz os números. Nada é calculado ou estimado quando a informação não existe; resultados por WO ficam como foram publicados.

Sequências

Participação seguida = edições consecutivas do campeonato. 2019 e 2022 são consecutivas, porque não houve campeonato em 2020 e 2021.
Nos anos com classificação incompleta, a ausência do nome não interrompe a sequência (o botonista pode ter jogado sem aparecer na lista), mas o ano só é somado se o nome aparece.

Pessoas e estados

Cada botonista é identificado por um código (nome padronizado + estado de estreia), para acompanhar a mesma pessoa mesmo quando o nome é impresso de formas diferentes ou ela muda de estado. A identificação é automática e pode ter erros, principalmente entre homônimos.
“Estado que defendia no ano” é a UF impressa na classificação daquela edição. “Estado de origem” é a UF da primeira participação do botonista no Brasileiro — o histórico não informa o estado de nascimento.
69 linhas não têm UF no histórico (por exemplo em 1997 e em tabelas de base de 2002) e entram em “Outros”.
Atletas estrangeiros aparecem com a sigla do país seguida de * (HU*, Hungria; JP*, Japão): entram em “Outros” e não contam como estado representado.

Encontrou algo errado? Avise por aqui ou deixe um comentário no fim da página — as correções são feitas na base de dados e aparecem aqui na atualização seguinte.

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
First things first
In my daily routine as a data scientist, I noticed that in my production pipeline the LGBMRegressor model was not running with success on GPU inside the container. After that, I decided to take a look on how was the Dockerfile:
FROM nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-runtime-ubuntu24.04
# INSTALL CONDA

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y wget
RUN wget https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-py39_24.11.1-0-Linux-x86_64.sh
RUN bash Miniconda3-py39_24.11.1-0-Linux-x86_64.sh -b -p /opt/conda
ENV PATH="/opt/conda/bin:${PATH}"

# CREATE PIPELINE CONDA ENV

WORKDIR /usr/src/pipeline
COPY ./gpu-time-series-env.yaml .
RUN conda env create -f gpu-time-series-env.yaml
ENV CONDA_OVERRIDE_CUDA=12.2

SHELL ["conda", "run", "-n", "gpu_time_series", "/bin/bash", "-c"]

RUN conda install -c conda-forge tensorflow-gpu=2.17.0 lightgbm=4.6.0
RUN conda install conda-forge::flash-attn-layer-norm==2.6.3
RUN pip install xgboost==3.0.5

# COPY CODE AND RUN

COPY . .
CMD [ \
    "bash", "-c", \
    "source /opt/conda/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && \
    conda activate gpu_time_series && \
    conda config --set channel_priority strict && \
    python3 main.docker.py" \
]

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
Some Concepts (you can skip it)
Before dive into the problem I will give some definition of containers, docker and virtual machine (VM).
Containers are a way to encapsulate your application and dependencies that can be installed in a different machine without the need to install every instruction manually. Unlike Virtual Machines (VMs), it does not virtualize the hardware, neither operates in a new Operational System (OS). Instead, it shares the same kernel of the host machine, with no overhead when it is operating inside a linux (that’s also way I use Ubuntu), or a little overhead with Windows (it needs to be use WSL and Hypervision) or MacOS.
In Data Science, we need a lighter, fast and isolated piece of software, that’s way containers are handy. We do not need to have another entire system to our disposal.
When we run FROM: ubuntu:24.04 in Dockerfile we are not installing a fresh new Ubuntu for that container. We are only installing some parts of the Ubuntu, such as bash, apt and /usr, /etc folders, while having the same kernel of the host (it is not even necessary to have the same version of the linux, as long as the kernel supports it).
Lastly, but not least, Docker is a tool that manages the containers :). Dockerfile is the filename used to create an image, that containers can be created from it.

Command definitions in the Docker

COPY Transfers files and directories from your host machine (the build context) into the container’s filesystem during the build phase. It runs in build time
RUN runs on files inside the container
CMD sets the default command that executes automatically when the container starts running. It does not execute during the build process. It runs in Runtime
SHELL changes the default shell used to execute subsequent RUN, CMD and ENTRYPOINT instructions during the build. Linux containers use [“/bin/sh”, “-c”]. It runs in build configuration.

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
How everything got solved:
Considering that solving the problem only for lightgbm, would leave many problems behind, I decided to take one by one.

LightGBM

First of all, I put back all packages inside the conda, because I wanted to use conda the single source of truth, and it would guarantee that its solver would not break in the Dockerfile.
Then, I realized that lightgbm installs two libraries:

liblightgbm which is the C++ code;
lightgbm which is the Python API.


Since one of them was installed by conda-forge channel, and another by defaults., it created a version mismatch between then, which did not make possible to use the GPU inside the container. Therefore, I reinstalled them using only conda-forge, which is the recommended channel nowadays.

⚠️ GOOD PRACTICE ALERT: Use only a single channel when creating a conda env.

In addition to that, conda-forge itself has three different ways to install its package: cuda, gpu or cpu. It also needs to be specified in the yaml. In this case, I did liblightgbm=4.6.0=cuda* and lightgbm=4.6.0=cuda*. cuda because is more modern than gpu. It guarantees that conda-forge would pick a cuda version of this library. I could be even more restrict to enforce cuda to be a specific version, but I set it loose.


flash-attn
It was also a bit pain, because it needs to be installed after pytorch (that’s way it was out of the conda env) once I installed from pip, which has an import pytorch after installation.

The good news is that after installing from conda-forge, this pre-installation process does not exists, and made possible to include it inside the conda env, with no ordering needed.



Cuda versions
What I realized is that inside the (gpu-time-series-env.yaml), I already had cuda (cuda-version=12.9). Therefore, it allowed me to get rid of image that install cuda and the CONDA_OVERRIDE_CUDA env var. Letting conda be the only one responsible by solving cuda.
It could be a good solution, but it would not last long because my cuda environment was created using conda env export --no-builds, which only describes the environment, i.e. it lists the packages that I want. But it does not specify the builds, because these builds are from the respective machine where I am using, and may not be compatible inside the machine I need to install it (I had problem with it before installing using only conda env export).
To solve this, I created the conda-lock.yaml file from conda-lock package, that locks the exact dependency resolution needed to reproduce an environment. It solves conda versioning of the packages and save it with all information needed to a fresh install. In order to create this file I also had to create the file virtual-packages.yaml:
subdirs:
  linux-64:
    packages:
      __glibc: "2.28"
      __cuda: "12.9"
which specicies the cuda version, allowing the new image to know that cuda is available (just like CONDA_OVERRIDE_CUDA beore).


Pinned ubuntu image
When we just use FROM ubuntu:24.04, even though we pin the operational system, it keeps receiving patch updates, and can make our code to break unexpectedly. In order to overcome this, there are two main ways of doing it:

Using the manifest digest, which it is a sha key, not human readable, in this casesha256:33ceb71981b602c1a7443a53469e4dba065f7503eab3078a2d7a57a2ab987517; or
Using <name_of_ubuntu>-<published_date>, in this case noble-20260810

I used the second option, of course, because it is human readable.


Channels strict and conda lock
Once all packages are from conda-forge:

I no longer need conda config --set channel_priority strict
I no longer need miniconda (which has default and conda-forge channels available):

I switched to miniforge which is the miniconda of only conda-forge channel, being lightweight.



Pinning miniforge
I have also pinned miniforge to a version specific, because it will install Python on your container image; and an update on Python that may result an update to the latest miniforge can also break your software.

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
Optimized Dockerfile
After applying all theses changes, I was able to come up with the following solution:
FROM ubuntu:noble-20260810

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y wget && \
    wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/download/26.3.2-3/Miniforge3-26.3.2-3-Linux-x86_64.sh -O /tmp/miniforge.sh && \
    bash /tmp/miniforge.sh -b -p /opt/conda && rm /tmp/miniforge.sh

ENV PATH="/opt/conda/bin:${PATH}"

# CREATE PIPELINE CONDA ENV
WORKDIR /usr/src/pipeline

COPY conda-lock.yml .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir conda-lock && \
    conda-lock install --micromamba --name gpu_time_series conda-lock.yml && \
    pip uninstall -y conda-lock && \
    conda clean -afy && \
    rm -rf /opt/conda/pkgs/cache/* ~/.cache/pip ~/.cache/conda-lock ~/.mamba ~/.local/share/mamba

# Activate environment for RUN commands
SHELL ["conda", "run", "-n", "gpu_time_series", "/bin/bash", "-c"]

COPY . .

CMD [ \
    "bash", "-c", \
    "source /opt/conda/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && \
    conda activate gpu_time_series && \
    python3 main.docker.py" \
    ]
Which is 20% faster to build and a 70% lighter image than the previous Dockerfile because:

Ubuntu and miniforge are lighter;
I have used micromamba as well cleared all cache from package installation;
Started using .dockerignore.

title: How I made LGBM to work in GPU inside Docker and decrease image size by 70%
text:
Next Steps

Happy coding!

title: Is Python an Interpreted language?
text:
When I decided to study it, I felt the same as Naruto learning the Rasengan: It was difficult to learn: Naruto took 3 years to learn; and I took 10 😂, since I firstly heard the words “interpreted”/“compiled” language when I was learning R.
Python, itself is an interpreted language, and there are many nuances that I want to discuss.
Let’s start by defining what is a programming language.

title: Is Python an Interpreted language?
text:
1 Programming language
A programming language can be defined by two main pillars:

Specification (Rules):

Syntax: how the code is written; some languages may be more verbose than others. For example, in C you need to define the type of each variable and finish the line with ;. Whereas Python does not require it, but indentation is obligatory for your code to run.
Semantics: It defines basic operations, such as, the operator +, does what we think it does: add two values together (in case of floats/ints) or concatenate two lists in Python.
Data Types & Core concepts: In Python, we have dict, but we do not have dataframes; R is the opposite.

Implementation:

Machines do not understand source code, only binary machine code (0s and 1s). So, for every programming language, a tool is necessary that translates the source code into binary code that can be:

Compiler: It will translate upfront the entire source code into a standalone binary executable. It is a characteristic of C, Rust and Go programming languages;
Interpreter: It will translate the source code into binary code at the runtime line by line. This is the primary implementation strategy for Python, JavaScript and R.

title: Is Python an Interpreted language?
text:
2 Python’s implementation
What makes a programming language interpreted or compiled is its implementation. Python has different implementations, such as:

Nuitka and Cython make the Python a compiled language, so, all machine code is known ahead of time.
PyPy uses JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation: it takes the Python source file, converts it to bytecode1, and directly compiles it into machine code during the runtime (not ahead of time). It is a just-in-time compiler, rather than an ahead-of-time compiler.
CPython, the official implementation, first compiles the Python source code to bytecode2. Then the Python Virtual Machine (PVM) - itself a program in C - reads that bytecode and hands each instruction off to an already-existing C function inside the interpreter that carries it out. That’s why Python is known as an “interpreted language”.


Bytecode plays a vital role here: Python caches the first time a module is imported, saving it as a .pyc file so it does not need to be recompiled on every subsequent import.
It never translates Python code into machine code directly; instead, the PVM executes the bytecode by invoking the corresponding pre-compiled C function for each instruction.

Finally, what makes a language interpreted or compiled is the implementation, not the language itself.
This picture describes the whole process of executing Python source code:







There is more! Keep reading Part 2!
Happy Coding!

title: Is Python an Interpreted language?
text:
Footnotes


bytecode is an intermediate low-level code that can be read and interpreted by a machine, being originated by a source code.↩︎
you can inspect the bytecode of any Python function by calling dis.dis(<your_function>), see is python a dynamic language.↩︎

title: Concurrency and Parallelism in Python
text:
Once upon a time, computers had a single core that could run only one stream of instructions at a time, so programs were executed strictly sequentially.
Nowadays, computers have multiple physical cores, and each physical core can expose more than one logical core (hardware thread) through Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT), which Intel calls Hyper-Threading. On Intel and AMD consumer processors, this is usually 2 hardware threads per core, while some server processors (such as IBM POWER) go up to 8. You can check how many logical cores your machine has with os.cpu_count() in Python.
Therefore, it is worth taking advantage of all this power and running more than one thing at a time.
Before going further, it is important to separate two terms that are often used interchangeably:
Parallelism is a special case of concurrency: every parallel program is concurrent, but not every concurrent program is parallel. That is why the Python documentation groups all the tools below under the name Concurrent Execution.
In Python, we have three main ways of running code concurrently:
And a high-level interface on top of the first two: concurrent.futures.
In order to choose one of these methods, we first need to understand the problem we are trying to solve, and pick the right tool for it. The main question is: is my code waiting for something (I/O-bound), or is it busy computing (CPU-bound)?

title: Concurrency and Parallelism in Python
text:
1 Multithreading
A multithreaded program is a program that uses multiple threads to run its tasks. A thread is the unit that actually executes your code, and every process has at least one thread (the main thread). All the threads of a process share the same memory space, and in Python they are real OS threads, which means the operating system decides when each one runs.
The downside of multithreading in Python is the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock): a lock that allows only a single thread to execute Python bytecode at a time inside a process. So, even if you start 8 threads on an 8-core machine, only one of them is running Python code at any given moment, while the others wait for the GIL to be released.
Since Python 3.13 there is an optional free-threaded build (PEP 703) in which the GIL can be disabled, and since Python 3.14 this build is officially supported (PEP 779). In this build, threads can truly run in parallel. The trade-offs are that some third-party libraries may not support it yet, and that a program using a single thread runs slower on the free-threaded build than on the regular one (about 40% slower in 3.13, reduced to roughly 5-10% in 3.14), because the interpreter needs extra internal work to stay safe without the GIL.
Be aware that the GIL does not protect you from race conditions. It protects the interpreter’s internal state, not your program’s logic: an operation such as counter += 1 is made of several bytecode instructions, and a thread can be switched in the middle of them. Whenever threads modify shared data, you should protect it with a threading.Lock. Without the GIL, these bugs simply become more likely to show up.
Therefore, in the usual scenario, threads run concurrently, not in parallel: only one executes Python code, while the others wait.
The advantage of multithreading shows up when the program performs Input/Output (I/O) operations, such as waiting for a server to respond, reading a file, or querying a database. While a thread is blocked waiting for I/O, it releases the GIL, and another thread can run. The threads then operate in an interleaved way. For example:

Thread 1 sends a request to the server and waits for the response (it releases the GIL, and the OS schedules another thread).
Thread 2 sends its request to the server and also waits for the response.
Thread 1 receives the data from the server and finishes.
Thread 2 receives the data from the server and finishes.

Instead of waiting for two responses one after the other, the program waits for both at the same time.
Even though the threads are not running at the same instant, this is the impression the user gets, because the switches between threads happen very fast. Even when no thread is waiting for I/O, Python asks the running thread to release the GIL every 5 milliseconds by default (see sys.getswitchinterval()), so that every thread gets its turn.
Many C extensions, such as NumPy, also release the GIL during heavy computations, so threads can be useful in these cases too.

title: Concurrency and Parallelism in Python
text:
2 Multiprocessing
When we use multiprocessing, the main program (the parent process, whose ID you get with os.getpid()) starts several child processes (from inside a child, os.getppid() returns the parent’s ID). Each child process has its own Python interpreter, its own memory, and its own GIL. Therefore, the processes do not compete for a single lock, and they can run truly in parallel, at the same time, on different cores.
This is useful when you have a CPU-bound operation (heavy calculations, data processing, model training) and want to use all the cores of your machine. You can start more processes than you have cores, but the benefit is achieved when each process gets its own core; beyond that, the processes just take turns.
The price to pay is that processes do not share memory. The data needs to be serialized (pickled) and sent to each process, and the results need to be sent back to the parent. Starting a process is also much more expensive than starting a thread. So, for light operations, or for I/O-bound tasks, multiprocessing can be slower than multithreading and will use more memory.
A good experiment is to watch how many processes are running on your OS.

2.1 Threads and processes in the OS
For example, take a look at this htop screenshot:

We have 198 tasks, which in this case means processes, and they are using 1526 threads in total, but only 1 is running at this moment (the others are sleeping, waiting for something to happen).
So, an OS can start as many processes as it needs (regardless of the number of cores), and each process can have multiple threads associated with it. Your machine is, all the time, running a multiprocess and multithreaded workload.

title: Concurrency and Parallelism in Python
text:
3 Futures
The concurrent.futures module provides a single, high-level interface for both approaches above: ThreadPoolExecutor (a pool of threads) and ProcessPoolExecutor (a pool of processes). You submit a task to a pool of workers, and you immediately receive a Future: an object that represents a result that is not ready yet. Later, you call .result() to get the value, waiting for it if needed.
The nice part is that switching from threads to processes is usually a matter of changing a single line, since both executors have the same API (submit, map, and so on). It does not add a new way of running code, it just makes threads and processes easier to use.

title: Concurrency and Parallelism in Python
text:
4 Asyncio
Asyncio - Asynchronous I/O (Input/Output) - is a Python library for writing concurrent code using the async and await syntax. As the name says, it is also aimed at I/O operations, but differently from multithreading, it runs on a single thread. Since there is only one thread, the GIL is not a concern here. Instead of the OS deciding when to switch, we mark in the code the points where the program is waiting (with await), and at those points it can jump to another task.
It is like going to a coffee shop and ordering a machine coffee. The clerk presses the button to make the coffee, and instead of waiting for it to be ready, they take the order of the next customer. After that, they go back to the machine and collect the first coffee, which is ready by now.
Each of these routines is, in Python, a coroutine: a function defined with async def, that can pause its execution and resume later from the same point. The single clerk orders the coffee, awaits for it to be ready, checks whether there is another customer, charges them, and then returns to the machine to collect the coffee for the first customer.
The one coordinating all of this is the event loop, managed by asyncio (usually started with asyncio.run()). It keeps track of all the tasks and, whenever a task hits an await, it resumes another task that is ready to continue.
The main advantage over multithreading is that the switching is cooperative: we tell the event loop exactly where the code can be paused, instead of letting the OS interrupt the threads at any point. This avoids many race conditions, and since tasks are much lighter than threads, a single program can handle thousands of simultaneous connections.
The disadvantage is that the whole code needs to be asynchronous: a single blocking call (such as time.sleep() or requests.get()) freezes the whole event loop, since there is only one thread. Therefore, the libraries you use also need to support asynchronous code (for example, aiohttp or httpx instead of requests), and many of them do not. When there is no alternative, you can send the blocking call to a thread with asyncio.to_thread().

title: Concurrency and Parallelism in Python
text:
5 Conclusion



Table 1: Summary of the three approaches












Multithreading
Multiprocessing
Asyncio




Python module
threading, concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor
multiprocessing, concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor
asyncio


Concurrent or parallel?
Concurrent (parallel only in the free-threaded build)
Parallel
Concurrent


Unit of work
OS thread
OS process
Coroutine (task)


Who decides when to switch?
The OS (preemptive)
The OS (each process runs on its own)
The code, at each await (cooperative)


Affected by the GIL?
Yes, one thread runs Python at a time
No, each process has its own GIL
Not relevant, it is a single thread


Memory
Shared between threads
Separate for each process; data must be pickled
Shared, single thread


Startup cost
Low
High
Very low


Race conditions
Yes, needs locks
Rare, since nothing is shared by default
Fewer, switches only at await


Best for
I/O-bound tasks, or C extensions that release the GIL
CPU-bound tasks
I/O-bound tasks with many connections


Main drawback
GIL limits CPU-bound code
Memory and communication overhead
Every library must be async






As a rule of thumb: if your code is waiting, use threads or asyncio; if your code is computing, use processes.

title: Concurrency and Parallelism in Python
text:
6 Glossary
I have included some terminology that may or may not be directly related to the text, but that may help with a general understanding:

Concurrency: two tasks make progress in the same period of time, but not necessarily at the same instant.
Parallelism: two tasks are executed at the same instant.
Race condition: when more than one thread accesses the same piece of memory at the same time, and at least one of them modifies it, so the result depends on the order in which the threads happen to run.
Synchronous code: runs a task until it is finished, and only then starts the next one.
Asynchronous code: can start a task, pause it, and later resume from where it stopped, until it is finished.
Future: an object representing a result that will be available in the future. The computation may start now or later.
Lazy evaluation: an expression is only evaluated when its value is needed.
Future vs. lazy evaluation: a lazy value does nothing until it is requested. A Future, on the other hand, is usually computed in parallel or concurrently with the rest of the code, at some moment between its creation and the moment the code needs (or waits for) the result. So, it can run in a thread or in a process.
Promise: a commitment that a computation will be performed and its result delivered. The term is common in JavaScript; in Python, the closest concept is the Future.
with: guarantees that the cleanup code of a context manager (closing a file, releasing a lock, shutting down an executor) is executed when the block ends, even if an exception is raised inside it.
Generator: a Python function returns a generator when it uses yield instead of return. Its values are produced lazily, one at a time.
yield from and await: ways of consuming another generator or coroutine, respectively. await can only be used inside an asynchronous function (async def). yield from was used by the old generator-based coroutines, which were removed in Python 3.11.
aiohttp.ClientSession: manages HTTP requests asynchronously, without blocking the event loop.
requests: a blocking library; it runs requests synchronously.
async: defines that a function is asynchronous (a coroutine).
await: pauses the current coroutine until the awaited operation finishes, letting the event loop run other tasks in the meantime.
Task: a unit of work that the computer must execute.
Worker: “the guy” that executes the tasks. It can be a thread or a process, for example. What a worker is depends on the context of your code.
I/O-bound: a task whose time is mostly spent waiting for input/output (network, disk, database).
CPU-bound: a task whose time is mostly spent computing.

title: The day that I decided to stop using Windows
text:
Introduction
During my undergraduate studies, my professor Paulo Justiniano always incentivized the students for using any Linux distribution on their machines. The reasons were vast, but I will give the details later on.
I never tried it before because:

I was comfortable using Windows because I used this operational system on my internship and at home
I did not have a personal laptop at the beginning of university.

On my last year of college, I bought one with Windows pre installed, and I was using as it is (knowing that migrating to Ubuntu would be better). But the day came!

title: The day that I decided to stop using Windows
text:
The Day
I remember like it was today. It was during the time that everyone was migrating from Windows 8.1 to 10. I was working on a report, had worked the full day on it, and then I decided to migrate to Windows 10. The migration finished successfully, I opened the file, started typing a few more words, and then, out of nothing my report became corrupted:







I could not save or send my report to anywhere, and I received the famous blue screen:







I had to turn off and on my PC using the power button, but I could not see the original content of the file anymore. It was gone. At the same time, I downloaded the Mint iso file, burned it onto a pen drive, installed it and started using.
It was not only flowers at the beginning, as usual. My friend Augusto Colombo helped me in the lab to install and do the basics. Some weeks later, and I did not like the Mint, so I swap to Ubuntu.

title: The day that I decided to stop using Windows
text:
The redemption



With Ubuntu everything fell into place. All the troubles that I had when tried a fresh install on Mint it was solved on Ubuntu, and I could fix by myself.
It really represents the meaning of Ubuntu, from Nguni languages: “I am what I am because of who we all are”. Ever since then I use ubuntu on my personal laptop and in my current job. It is so amazing.
It gives many advantages for me compared to the time I had Windows:

I know how to do a fresh install when needed.
It is free to use. Don’t need to pay any license.
It hardly enters a virus.
The performance does not go down over time.
There is a full community open to help.
Due to the fact that most of installation is made via CLI, it opens your mind to shell, to automate your repetitive tasks.
The hard drive is portable. I can remove from my PC and plug it into another. It will not crash.

When we talk specifically about Data Science tasks, I can list:

Python is pre-installed on Ubuntu.
Docker runs natively on Linux.
Almost every server in the world uses a distro based on Linux. Choosing a server on EC2, it is like to choose which Linux you want to use. Using Ubuntu daily means that when I need to access servers, I am more familiar with the operational system.
Installation of tools for data science such as R, Python, dependencies are usually easily handed on Ubuntu.
A common task on a DS work is to tell the path where you files are. If you are on Windows, you need to copy the path, paste on a Editor and make the backslashes into forward slashes, or double it. With Ubuntu, you do not. You use as it is.

The only thing that sometimes I miss on Ubuntu is the Office package. But using Libre Office is lighter, free and it is a good alternative full of customizations.

title: The day that I decided to stop using Windows
text:
Considerations
I am aware that the latest Windows release have become better, such that, WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) became available and Windows 11 is stable now. From another point of view, Ubuntu has now Steam for gaming, but it is still not ideal when you want a full gaming experience. In the end of the day, it is always a matter of which operational system suits you best: just like for designers that love Apple.
With all that given, it would be nice if we could choose the operational system that fits better our role, instead of going to the usual operational system.
Maybe we can reach a day that:



Leave in the comments any thoughts about it!
Happy coding!
